slo_title: Apply mathematical techniques to solve heat equations in one-dimensional settings.

mcq.q: The steady state temperature of a rod of length l whose ends are kept at \(30 ^0\) and \(40 ^0\) is,
The one dimensional heat equation is,
In one dimensional heat equation \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \) , \(\alpha^2\) stand for,
The proper solution of one dimensional heat equation \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \) is,
How many initial and boundary conditions are required to solve \(\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \) ,

sq.q: \(\text{State the one-dimensional heat equation and derive it from first principles.}\)
answer: \(\text{Heat equation: } \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}, \text{ where } \alpha^2 = \frac{k}{c\rho}.\)
\(\text{Consider a thin bar of cross-section A. Let } u(x,t) \text{ be temperature.}\)
\(\text{Heat in element: } Q = c \rho A \Delta x \Delta u. \text{ Rate of increase: } c\rho A \Delta x \frac{\partial u}{\partial t}.\)
\(\text{Heat inflow at x: } R_1 = -kA \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_x, \text{ outflow at } x+\Delta x: R_2 = -kA \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_{x+\Delta x}.\)
\(\text{Net inflow } = kA \left[\left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_{x+\Delta x} - \left(\frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\right)_x\right]. \text{ Equate and take limit to get heat equation.}\)

sq.q: \(\text{Using separation of variables, solve } \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2} \text{ and obtain the general solution. Why is } u=(A\cos\lambda x+B\sin\lambda x)e^{-\alpha^2\lambda^2 t} \text{ chosen for transient problems?}\)
answer: \(\text{Separate: } \frac{T'}{\alpha^2 T} = \frac{X''}{X} = k. \text{ For } k<0 \ (k=-\lambda^2), \text{ get } T'+\alpha^2\lambda^2 T=0, X''+\lambda^2 X=0.\)
\(\text{Solve: } T = Ce^{-\alpha^2\lambda^2 t}, X = A\cos\lambda x + B\sin\lambda x.\)
\(\text{This solution decays with time, representing transient (unsteady) state. For steady state, temperature becomes independent of time.}\)

lq.q: \(\text{Derive the three possible solutions of the one-dimensional heat equation $\frac{\partial u}{\partial t} = \alpha^2 \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x^2}$}\\ \text{by separation of variables. Explain why the exponential decay solution is suitable for transient problems.}\)
answer: Step Marks \(\text{Assume \(u(x,t)=X(x)T(t).\) Substitute: \(XT' = \alpha^2 X''T.\)}\) (1 Mark) \(\text{Separate: \(X''/X = T'/(\alpha^2T) = k\) (constant).}\) (2 Marks) \(\text{Case \(k > 0\) (\(k=\lambda^2\)): \(X'' - \lambda^2X=0\), \(T' - \alpha^2\lambda^2T=0\) \(\Rightarrow\) solutions: \(X = Ae^{\lambda x}+Be^{-\lambda x}\), \(T = Ce^{\alpha^2\lambda^2 t}\) (growing exponential in time).}\) (2 Marks) \(\text{Case \(k < 0\) (\(k=-\lambda^2\)): \(X'' + \lambda^2X=0\), \(T' + \alpha^2\lambda^2T=0\) \(\Rightarrow\) solutions: \(X = A \cos(\lambda x) + B \sin(\lambda x)\), \(T = Ce^{-\alpha^2\lambda^2 t}\) (decaying exponential).}\) (2 Marks) \(\text{Case \(k = 0\): \(X''=0\), \(T'=0\) \(\Rightarrow\) \(X = Ax+B\), \(T = C\) (constant in time).}\) (1 Mark) \(\text{For transient heat flow, temperature should decay to steady state as \(t\to\infty.\)}\) (2 Marks) Solution with positive exponential in time is physically unrealistic (temperature blows up). (2 Marks) \(\text{Constant solution (\(k=0\)) corresponds to steady state.}\) (1 Mark) \(\text{Thus decaying exponential (\(k\) negative) is appropriate for transient problems.}\) (2 Marks)
